source.title: Scaling Laws Behind Code Understanding Model
source.authors: Jiayi Lin; Hande Dong; Yutao Xie; Lei Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some appendix references are unresolved, but the study's main results and relevant figures are included.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling relationships for masked-token prediction in code-understanding encoder models, a code-training setting distinct from the original language-model scaling experiments. It also tests scale trends on downstream code tasks.
record.gate_note: The scaling-loss and downstream scaling plots report results only as figures; no plotted coordinates are stated numerically in the text. The paper's comparative CoLSBERT results and probing-task results do not isolate a scaling relationship, so they are not recorded as rows. The paper states that CoLSBERT's pretraining data, model size, and compute were enlarged together, but reports no held-out pretraining loss for that run.
record.test_reason: The study pretrains code-understanding transformer encoders from scratch with masked-token prediction. It varies training data, model size and compute separately, and reports held-out masked-token test error with power-law fits (Fig. 3). It also reports downstream code-search and clone-detection results across the same scales (Figs. 4–5). This is a new setting, bidirectional MLM on code, with direct results on V1 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that masked-token test error of code-understanding encoders falls as a power law in training data, model size and compute, so the scaling law holds for code understanding. Larger pretraining scale improves code search and clone detection, though not precisely following the power law. A 1.5B model (CoLSBERT) trained on 351B tokens beats prior code encoders. They also note a slowdown above 354M parameters, which they attribute to limited data. They leave joint scaling and compute-budget balancing to future work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a transformer encoder trained from scratch on code with a masked-token prediction objective, measuring masked-token test error rather than autoregressive language-model loss. It varies data, model size, and compute separately rather than testing compute-optimal joint allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The test-error decline slows beyond 354M parameters. The authors suggest that 1.8M samples may be insufficient to fully train larger models; they used Pre-LN to address degradation beyond 757M parameters. Clone-detection improvement is described as having a turning point.
record.code_released: not stated; the paper says it will release code and CoLSBERT when published
record.problems: Scaling-curve values are presented in figures without numeric coordinates in the text. The power-law experiments vary each dimension separately, and do not test their joint effects or compute-optimal allocation. The authors report a slowdown in test-error decline at larger model sizes and suggest the available training data may be insufficient.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows omitted for the tested scale series. Table 5 comparisons include models with differing pretraining methods and do not isolate a scale effect; probing results measure code-property classification rather than the claim versions.

untested.parts: Power-law behaviour over several orders of magnitude: the data sweep spans 8x, model size about 12x, compute about 6x. Autoregressive next-token loss. Each dimension is varied with the others fixed (data fixed at 1.8M samples), not with the others kept non-bottlenecking. No fitted exponents are reported numerically.
Whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss, i.e. any fitted downstream curve. Tasks other than code search and clone detection.

record.verdict_notes: All scaling values are figure-only, and no fitted exponents are given in the text. Uncertainty is shown only for test-error stability under random masking (Fig. 2); the scaling curves have no error bars. The compute and data sweeps both involve multi-epoch training on small corpora, which a reader comparing with V1/V3 studies should note. The size-sweep slowdown could be read as a bend away from a single power law (V7), but the authors attribute it to a data bottleneck, which is consistent with V1's 'not the bottleneck' caveat. It is therefore not labelled V7. Table 5 (CoLSBERT versus other models) and the probing results do not isolate scale and are rightly left out. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests masked-token test error for code-understanding encoders while varying data, model size, or compute separately. It does not test autoregressive next-token cross-entropy or show that the other two scale dimensions are never bottlenecks.
No held-out prediction test in which a power-law fit from small runs predicts the loss of substantially larger runs.
The study varies data, model size, and compute separately; it explicitly says their collective impact and budget-efficient balance are not explored.
No comparison holds parameter count fixed while varying depth, width, or other architecture details.
The study concerns code pretraining with a masked-token objective. It does not test image or video modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling laws.

The study tests downstream code-search and clone-detection performance against pretraining scale. It does not test whether downstream performance is predicted by pretraining loss, nor whether these trends generalize to other downstream task families.
The study does not compare fitting choices or published exponents, and does not report a systematic analysis of curves bending away from a power law. It notes a slower decline above 354M parameters.

rows.operation_detail: Train on The Stack data at the stated scale and measure masked-token test error.
rows.note: The authors report decreasing test error as training data grows and say the points align well with a power-law curve.
rows.check: The model is fixed at 124M and 100K steps (26B tokens seen). CSN-1x is about 1.88M functions, so the smaller data scales are trained for many epochs. The data sweep therefore mixes data size with repetition. It also spans only 8x, under one order of magnitude. The same caveat applies to loss-data-2x, -4x and -8x.

rows.note: The authors report a discernible slowdown in the decline above 354M parameters; Pre-LN was adopted to address degradation beyond 757M.
rows.check: The decline slows above 354M on a figure-only curve. The authors attribute this to the fixed 1.8M-sample training set, i.e. a data bottleneck. The text says degradation appeared beyond 757M and Pre-LN was used to mitigate it. It is unclear whether the 757M model itself used Pre-LN.

source_check.correct: Normalization at 757M is not explicitly specified: Section 3.3 reports degradation beyond 757M and employs Pre-LN as mitigation without identifying every affected checkpoint. For V1, state=cannot_determine: the slowdown above 354M occurs with potentially insufficient data.
source_check.problem: Pre-LN is not explicitly assigned to 757M; the possible data bottleneck prevents interpreting the slowdown as partial V1 scaling.

rows.subject: transformer-encoder
rows.operation_detail: Train for the stated number of iterations and measure masked-token test error.
rows.note: The authors report decreasing test error with more compute and say the values fit a power-law expression.
rows.check: The compute sweep varies only iterations on a fixed 124M model and fixed CodeSearchNet-training data. More compute here means more epochs over the same data, so it is a repeated-token sweep, not compute-optimal scaling. It spans about 6x (1.95e19 to 1.17e20 FLOPs). The same applies to the other loss-compute rows.

relationships.condition: Code MLM encoders: data sweep (1x–8x, 124M model), compute sweep (100K–600K steps, 124M model), and model size 124M–354M
relationships.reason: The authors report test error falling and aligning with log-log linear fits for data and compute, and for size up to 354M (loss-data-*, loss-compute-*, loss-size-124M/354M). The ranges are narrow and figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Test error decreased along log-log linear fits for data and compute, and for model size up to 354M parameters.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Code MLM encoders: data sweep (1x–8x, 124M model), compute sweep (100K–600K steps, 124M model), and model size 124M–354M
source_check.reason: Sections 3.2–3.4 report declining held-out masked-token loss and agreement with log-log linear fits. This supports the form locally; several-orders-of-magnitude behavior is untested.

relationships.condition: Model size above 354M at fixed 1.8M-sample training data and 100K steps
relationships.reason: The decline in test error visibly slows for the 757M and 1.5B models (loss-size-757M, loss-size-1.5B). The authors attribute this to insufficient data. These models also needed Pre-LN to avoid degradation, so the size curve is not a clean single power law.
relationships.display_finding: Test-error reductions slowed for the 757M and 1.5B models, which the authors attributed to insufficient data.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Model size above 354M at fixed 1.8M-sample training data and 100K steps
source_check.reason: V1 explicitly requires other resources not to bottleneck scaling. Section 3.3 suggests insufficient data as the explanation for the slowdown, without establishing a deviation under adequate data. The claim that both larger checkpoints needed Pre-LN is also not explicit.

relationships.condition: Fine-tuned code search (CodeSearchNet MRR) and clone detection (POJ-104 MAP@R) across data, size and compute scales
relationships.reason: The authors state performance improves with each scale dimension in Figs. 4–5 (search-* and clone-* rows).
relationships.display_finding: CodeSearchNet MRR and POJ-104 MAP@R improve as training data, model size and compute increase.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Fine-tuned code search (CodeSearchNet MRR) and clone detection (POJ-104 MAP@R) across data, size and compute scales
source_check.reason: Sections 4.2–4.3 and Figures 4–5 report consistent downstream improvement across all three scaling dimensions, supporting directional predictability in these settings; quantitative forecasting is untested.

relationships.condition: Predictability of downstream gains, especially clone detection
relationships.reason: The authors say downstream improvement does not precisely mirror the pretraining power law. Clone-detection gains show a turning point the authors liken to emergence (clone-* rows). Gains are monotone, but not shown to be predictable.
relationships.display_finding: Downstream improvements departed from the pretraining power law, with monotonic clone-detection gains showing a turning point described as emergence.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Predictability of downstream gains, especially clone detection
source_check.reason: V6 does not require downstream performance to follow the pretraining power-law form. A turning point and departure from that form do not establish failed predictability; the paper reports no quantitative prediction test.
